segments.text:
On the afternoon Amy Mihaljevic
disappeared, her mother received a phone
call
from her.

An FBI account describes Amy saying she
was okay.

Her mother believed she was calling from
home.

According to FBI Special Agent Vicki
Anderson, Amy was already with the person
who had taken her.

A familiar kind of check-in had given her
mother a mistaken picture of where
her daughter was.

Amy was ten years old and lived in Bay
Village, Ohio.
She enjoyed riding her bicycle.

In a family interview years later, her
father, Mark, remembered another part

of her life: the horses she rode, and the
way she played with their dog, Jake.

She had taught him to jump over her legs
as though he were a horse.

It is a small memory of Amy doing
something she loved, before her name
became
attached to an investigation.

Before October 27, 1989, someone had
contacted Amy with a
plan that involved her mother.

The caller said Amy could help choose a
gift to celebrate a promotion at work.

Bay Village Police place that contact
weeks before the disappearance.

The meeting was arranged for after school,
at a nearby shopping center.

The promise of a present for her mother
was the reason Amy had been given for
going there.
That Friday, Amy left school on foot.

The FBI says she went to Bay Village
Square and was seen outside a business,
apparently waiting for someone.

The police account describes witnesses
seeing her speak with an unidentified

man, then walk through the parking lot
with him.

No vehicle was seen, according to that
account.

The sighting establishes a public point in
the sequence, but it does not
reveal where Amy went afterward.
Her bicycle was still at school.

In a June 2026 interview, her brother,
Jason, recalled noticing it there
after his own classes ended.

News 5's account of the day says their
mother later found the bicycle at the

school and went to the police to report
Amy missing.

By then, the expectation that she was
safely home had given way to a
search for her.

Bay Village Police and the FBI began
investigating.

Public appeals spread beyond the shopping
center.

News 5's reporting describes
missing-person posters in shop windows and
flyers distributed around the region.

A local Pizza Hut put Amy's poster and a
composite drawing on its boxes.

Those efforts carried the appeal into
ordinary places where someone might

recognize her or remember the man seen
with her.

Inside the investigation, information also
accumulated.

The same reporting describes officers and
federal agents working through

leads, with a law-enforcement computer
system strained by the volume of
inquiries.

People were being asked to look back at
one afternoon, while investigators had
to organize what came in.

The public search continued, but Amy did
not return home.

On February 8, 1990, a jogger found Amy's
body in a field in
rural Ashland County.

She was wearing the clothing in which she
had last been seen.

The search for a missing child had become
an investigation into her death.

The discovery gave investigators another
location to examine, beyond the
shopping center where she had disappeared.

Some of the things believed to have been
with her were never recovered.

The FBI lists a turquoise horse earring,
black ankle boots and a black leather
binder.

Those objects remain part of its public
appeal.

They are details someone might recognize,
but the published record does not
establish what happened to them.

Their absence cannot explain, by itself,
who took Amy or where she was
killed.

Years later, investigators asked the
public to look closely at another object.

At a 2016 news conference, authorities
displayed a homemade-looking curtain

found in the field where Amy's body had
been discovered.

News 5 reported a connection between hair
on the curtain and the family's dog.

The appeal was for recognition of the
textile: where it might have come from,
or who might have made it.
The release brought responses.

Cleveland 19 reported that the
prosecutor's office received calls and
tips

afterward, and that law enforcement was
following them up.

The curtain offered a possible connection
between a physical object and

information someone outside the
investigation might hold.

Its owner and origin were still questions;
the public release did not announce
that either had been established.

The investigation also continued through
interviews and renewed publicity.

In a report marking thirty years since Amy
disappeared, FBI Special Agent

Lisa Hack described more than a hundred
interviews during her six years
working on the case.
She said the files filled seventy volumes.

The FBI had also put up billboards around
Cleveland and in neighboring states,
asking again for information.

Those were accounts of continuing work,
not a solved case.

In 2021, Bay Village Sergeant Edward
Chapman described a further
reason for examining the curtain.

He told News 5 that testing had identified
Amy's hair on it.

Investigators again asked whether anyone
recognized the unusual, apparently
handmade textile.

The new statement strengthened their
public explanation for its relevance.

It did not supply a public account of
where the crime occurred or identify the
person responsible.

The next reported testing developments
involved Amy's clothing.

In 2024, police said retesting had
detected male DNA, but the
amount was too small to create a profile.

That distinction matters: detecting
material and producing a usable profile
were different outcomes.

Investigators were hoping that more
sensitive procedures might eventually
allow further work on the sample.

They had not announced an identification
from it.

Another round of work involved separate
hairs.

News 5 reported that an FBI laboratory had
noticed hairs on evidence slides

previously thought to contain clothing
fibers.

They were sent to a private laboratory in
California for testing.

Chapman cautioned that the hairs did not
necessarily belong to the person

responsible, and that contamination was
possible after years of handling.

These were separate from the small DNA
sample on Amy's clothing.

In January 2026, Cleveland 19 reported a
setback in that hair
testing.

Detective Sergeant Jay Elish said Astrea
Forensics could not obtain a
profile from the submitted hairs.

The material was likely too small or too
degraded.

Investigators were continuing with DNA
work, but this particular effort had
not produced the result they wanted.

That outcome concerned the hairs; it did
not erase the separate clothing-DNA
finding.

By June, Police Chief Robert Gillespie was
describing the resources needed to
keep testing evidence.

He told Cleveland 19 that work was
continuing, although he could not discuss
every item being tested.

He explained that the Amy Fund
supplemented other funding so
investigators

could respond when testing opportunities
arose.

Bay Village's own community announcement
also describes the fund as supporting

investigative costs, including DNA
testing.

Financial support helps that work
continue; it is not a test result.

As of our October 16, 2026 source check,
Bay Village's public case

page describes the investigation as
ongoing.

Police still ask for help identifying the
curtain and blanket.

The FBI continues to offer a reward of up
to twenty-five thousand dollars for

information leading to the arrest and
conviction of those responsible for
Amy's death.

These remain public requests for
information, with the case unresolved in
the
sources reviewed.

For Amy's family, those records sit
alongside memories of a child.

In the thirty-year interview, her father
described still thinking about her
several times a week.

The bicycle, the time with Jake, the
things she enjoyed: those belong to

Amy's life, beyond the evidence left
behind.
Amy is a daughter and a sister.

The public appeal remains open, and the
effort to find answers continues.
